Intimidate

/in-TIM-uh-dayt/ — stress on second syllable · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To intimidate someone is to frighten or unsettle them, often to make them back down or obey.

The team's huge defenders intimidate opponents before the game even starts.

Worked Example

A boxing champion enters the ring early, staring down her nervous opponent across the canvas, rolling her shoulders and glowering—clearly using her size and presence to intimidate.

The champion's goal is to make her opponent feel unsettled and frightened so they lose confidence. That calculated attempt to frighten someone into a weaker position—that's exactly what intimidate means. 'Scare' alone doesn't capture the deliberate intent to control or dominate.

How Intimidate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

frighten

frighten: make someone feel sudden fear

bully

bully: repeatedly pick on someone weaker

threaten

threaten: promise harm to force someone's obedience

Antonyms

encourage

encourage: give someone confidence, hope, and support

reassure

reassure: calm someone's fears with comforting words

How Strong Is It? — frighten → intimidate → threaten → terrorize

frighten vs. intimidate

frighten vs. intimidate: Frighten is weaker than intimidate: frightening someone just scares them, while intimidating them uses fear as a tool to make them back down or obey.

threaten vs. intimidate

threaten vs. intimidate: Threaten is stronger than intimidate — to intimidate is to unsettle someone with fear, but to threaten is to openly promise harm if they don't do what you want.

terrorize vs. intimidate

terrorize vs. intimidate: Terrorize is far stronger than intimidate; intimidation makes someone hesitant and fearful, while terrorizing keeps a person trapped in constant, overwhelming fear.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, into (here intensifying: putting fear in) (Latin)

Root — tim

Root — tim: to fear (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, cause to be (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Intimidate builds on Latin timidus, 'fearful': in- ('into') plus tim- ('fear') plus the verb suffix -ate literally means 'to put fear into someone' — to frighten them into backing down or obeying.

Use the root in a new word: timid

Use the root in a new word: timid: A timid speaker is the easiest person to intimidate — both words grow from the same Latin root tim-, meaning 'fear.'

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / conversational

Intimidate is the right word when someone deliberately tries to make another person afraid in order to control them or make them back down. For plain fear without the intent, use 'frighten' or 'scare.' For repeated, cruel behavior, 'bully' is more precise.
